scenarios.query: Review this RFC (design doc): "RFC-0019: Public Webhooks API. We will replace the existing polling-based `/v1/sync` integration with a push-based webhooks system. Consumers register a callback URL; we POST event payloads as they occur." The RFC describes the event payload shape and registration flow, but has no section on API versioning strategy for the payload schema, no statement of delivery guarantees (at-least-once? exactly-once?) that would inform whether consumers need idempotency handling, and no migration/deprecation plan for consumers still on `/v1/sync`.
expected_behavior: Flags the missing versioning strategy for the webhook payload schema — once external consumers depend on a shape, changing it needs the same expand/contract discipline as any other public contract

Flags the absent delivery-guarantee statement (at-least-once vs. exactly-once) as a contract gap — consumers can't safely build idempotent handlers without knowing whether they'll ever receive a duplicate event

Flags the missing migration/deprecation plan for `/v1/sync` as a decision-record gap (this design doc proposes replacing an existing public integration, but names no sunset path) — demonstrates the lens firing on a design document, not only a diff

Flags the API as easy to misuse: `plan` and `interval` accept any string rather than being constrained to the actual valid set (an enum/typed set), so a typo like `"montly"` silently creates a malformed subscription instead of being rejected at the boundary
Flags `trial_days` accepting a negative value with no validation — nothing in the type or the handler makes an invalid combination (negative trial length) impossible

Flags `internal_priority_score` under "when in doubt, leave it out": nothing indicates this field is clearly needed by consumers, and once it ships as public surface it can't be safely removed even if it turns out no one should have been setting it
Notes the field exists internally is not a reason to expose it — the question is whether external consumers need it, not whether it happens to already be there

Flags the error responses as ad-hoc strings rather than a typed, stable contract — `"nope, cant do that"` is not a documented, machine-parseable error a consumer can branch on, and `repr(e)` on the catch-all leaks internal exception details and will change wording across code changes
Recommends a stable error code/type per failure case (e.g. `{"error": {"code": "insufficient_funds"}}`) that consumers can rely on not changing wording out from under them
